notes:
Task and constraints: Count words stretchable to match S by extending repeated-character runs.
Idea: Run-length encode the target and each candidate word, then compare their character sequences and counts.
Technique and why it applies: A target run can expand a shorter word run only when the target run has at least three copies; equal run lengths are always allowed.
Invariant: R and count store target run characters and lengths; each candidate's encoding is compared positionally.
Edge cases: RLE of an empty string yields an empty iterator pair, which may unpack unexpectedly; the problem normally provides nonempty strings.
Complexity: Each word is processed linearly, so total time is O(total characters) and temporary space is O(word length).

Task and constraints: Determine whether the first player wins the chalkboard XOR game.
Idea: Return true when the XOR of all values is zero or the number of values is even.
Technique and why it applies: The game-theoretic result is that zero total XOR is immediately winning, and even-length nonzero cases are also winning under optimal play.
Invariant: The expression evaluates the aggregate XOR and parity of the list length.
Edge cases: functools and operator are referenced without imports in the snippet, so it will fail unless they are defined externally.
Complexity: Computing XOR is O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Determine whether the first player wins the chalkboard XOR game.
Idea: Reduce the list using bitwise XOR and check whether the length is even.
Technique and why it applies: The known strategy result makes the first player winning when the initial XOR is zero or the number of elements is even.
Invariant: reduce(xor, nums) computes the aggregate XOR; the second condition checks parity.
Edge cases: The code imports reduce and xor explicitly. The problem normally supplies a nonempty list; reduce without an initializer would fail on empty input.
Complexity: The reduction is O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Count visits to every domain and all of its parent subdomains.
Idea: Split each count-domain record, then accumulate the count for each suffix domain.
Technique and why it applies: Walking labels from right to left builds the top-level domain and each progressively longer subdomain.
Invariant: output maps each generated domain string to the total visit count accumulated so far.
Edge cases: The code prints intermediate lists and domain strings, causing unwanted stdout output. Input records are assumed to contain a count and valid domain.
Complexity: Processing all domain labels takes O(total labels) time and O(number of distinct subdomains) space.

Task and constraints: Count visits to each domain and all suffix subdomains.
Idea: Split domains into labels and construct every suffix from right to left.
Technique and why it applies: Each suffix receives the record's visit count, so visits to a full domain also contribute to its parent domains.
Invariant: result maps each suffix domain to its cumulative count.
Edge cases: The implementation assumes standard space-separated count-domain input; dictionary iteration order does not affect correctness.
Complexity: Runtime is proportional to total domain-label processing, with O(U) space for U distinct suffixes.

Task and constraints: Find the maximum area among all triangles formed by three input points.
Idea: Enumerate every triple of points and compute its area using the shoelace determinant.
Technique and why it applies: The absolute determinant gives twice the triangle area, so multiplying by one half yields the candidate area.
Invariant: maxA stores the largest area seen across examined triples.
Edge cases: Collinear triples produce zero area. The method assumes at least three points for a meaningful triangle, but otherwise returns zero.
Complexity: There are O(n³) triples, giving O(n³) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Compute the largest triangle area from the given points.
Idea: Use three nested loops to enumerate every distinct index triple and apply the determinant formula.
Technique and why it applies: The shoelace expression computes twice the signed area; absolute value and multiplication by 0.5 produce a nonnegative area.
Invariant: result is the maximum area found so far.
Edge cases: Collinear points yield zero, and distinct indices allow duplicate coordinates if the input contains them.
Complexity: The triple loops take O(n³) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Maximize the sum of averages when splitting A into at most k nonempty groups.
Idea: Initialize each suffix's average, then use dynamic programming to try additional group boundaries.
Technique and why it applies: For each possible first group end, its average is added to the best value for the remaining suffix.
Invariant: dp[i] stores the best sum of averages for the suffix beginning at i using the number of groups processed so far.
Edge cases: The variable sum shadows Python's built-in name but does not break this method. The loop bounds enforce at most k groups.
Complexity: The nested loops take O(kn²) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of buses needed to travel from source to target.
Idea: Build a stop-to-routes graph and run BFS over reachable stops, marking buses and stops visited.
Technique and why it applies: Taking a bus reaches all its stops at one additional bus ride; BFS explores routes in increasing ride count.
Invariant: bfs contains stops paired with the number of buses taken, while seen_buses prevents reprocessing a route.
Edge cases: The class-scoped imports may be available through class lookup, but indentation around the target return appears invalid Python and must be fixed before execution.
Complexity: The route-stop graph and BFS use O(total route stops) time and space.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum buses needed to travel between source and target.
Idea: Map each stop to routes that serve it, then breadth-first search by number of buses taken.
Technique and why it applies: At each layer, every route reachable from a stop is explored, and unseen stops are queued for the next bus count.
Invariant: lookup prevents revisiting stops, while to_route maps each stop to its available routes.
Edge cases: The code removes a route from a stop's set while iterating that same set, which can raise a runtime error; pruning also risks losing route information.
Complexity: Time and space are proportional to route-stop incidences, but the mutation can make execution fail.

Task and constraints: Generate all valid coordinate pairs represented by a digit string with outer parentheses removed.
Idea: Split the digits into left and right parts, then generate valid decimal placements in each part.
Technique and why it applies: Leading zeros are forbidden for multi-digit integer parts and trailing zeros are forbidden in fractional parts.
Invariant: _splitToNums enumerates decimal interpretations for each digit substring.
Edge cases: The regex string uses slash delimiters as though Python supported JavaScript regex syntax; it likely fails to reject all-zero splits. re and itertools are also not imported.
Complexity: The number of generated candidates is exponential in digit-string length; storage is proportional to output.

Task and constraints: Generate all coordinate pairs consistent with the digit string and decimal-format rules.
Idea: Choose a split between coordinates and generate legal decimal placements for both substrings.
Technique and why it applies: A multi-digit integer part cannot start with zero, and a fractional part cannot end with zero.
Invariant: make yields candidate numeric strings for a selected digit segment; product combines left and right candidates.
Edge cases: The range bounds control all coordinate splits. The code assumes the input is wrapped in parentheses and contains digits only.
Complexity: Output can be exponential in input length, so time and space depend on the number of candidates.

Task and constraints: Find the fewest instructions for a race car to reach target using acceleration and reversal.
Idea: Run breadth-first search over position and speed states, expanding accelerate and reverse actions.
Technique and why it applies: Each instruction costs one step, so BFS finds the shortest instruction sequence when states are handled correctly.
Invariant: q contains candidate position-speed states, and steps is the BFS depth.
Edge cases: The queue uses pop(0), which is linear time; there is no visited set, so states may repeat and the search can grow excessively. The reverse condition is also specialized and should be validated.
Complexity: This implementation may explore exponentially many states and can be very slow; queue operations add linear overhead.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum race-car instructions to reach each target position up to target.
Idea: Use dynamic programming over target distances, based on the bit length of each distance.
Technique and why it applies: A run of k accelerations reaches 2^k-1; overshoot-and-reverse and undershoot-with-two-reversals provide alternative constructions.
Invariant: dp[i] stores the minimum instructions needed to reach distance i.
Edge cases: The recurrence uses previously computed smaller target distances and handles exact all-accelerate distances directly.
Complexity: The outer loop and inner reversal choices give O(target log target) time and O(target) space.

Task and constraints: Find the most frequent word in a paragraph excluding banned words.
Idea: Normalize punctuation and case, split into words, count frequencies, remove banned words, and return the most common remaining word.
Technique and why it applies: Counter tracks word frequencies; deleting banned keys ensures the maximum remaining count belongs to an allowed word.
Invariant: para_count stores frequencies after tokenization and banned-word removal.
Edge cases: The code uses class-level imports for string and Counter, which may be resolved through the class; if all words are banned, most_common(1)[0] fails.
Complexity: Tokenization and counting take O(text length) expected time and O(number of unique words) space.

Task and constraints: Return the most common non-banned word in the paragraph.
Idea: Lowercase and split the paragraph, count stripped tokens, and select the most frequent token not banned.
Technique and why it applies: The counter provides frequencies, while the scan keeps the allowed word with the largest count.
Invariant: result is the best allowed word encountered so far.
Edge cases: Only a limited punctuation set is stripped from token ends; internal punctuation and other punctuation may remain. An empty valid set returns an empty string.
Complexity: Counting and scanning take O(text length) expected time and O(unique words) space.

Task and constraints: Find the shortest reference encoding for all words using shared suffixes.
Idea: Build a trie from each word's characters in reverse order and sum lengths for leaf words.
Technique and why it applies: A word that is a suffix of another ends at a non-leaf trie node and need not be encoded separately.
Invariant: trie_root stores reversed suffix paths; tail_nodes remembers each word's terminal node and encoded length.
Edge cases: Duplicate words are removed first. Leaf detection correctly excludes words that are suffixes of longer words.
Complexity: Trie construction is O(total characters) expected time and space.

Task and constraints: Compute the minimum length encoding that represents all words with shared suffixes.
Idea: Deduplicate words, insert their reversed characters into a trie, and sum lengths for terminal leaves.
Technique and why it applies: A word whose reversed path ends before another path is a suffix of a longer word and shares its encoding.
Invariant: nodes records each word's terminal trie node; leaves contribute len(word)+1 for the separator.
Edge cases: The code imports reduce and functools, but reduce is unused. Duplicate words are removed before insertion.
Complexity: Trie work is O(total characters) expected time and space.

Task and constraints: For every character position, return its distance to the nearest occurrence of character c.
Idea: Collect all positions of c, then compare every string index against every occurrence.
Technique and why it applies: The minimum absolute index difference is the nearest distance; the running minimum is reset for each position.
Invariant: ch stores target-character indices, and res collects each computed distance.
Edge cases: If c does not occur, the method returns len(s) at every position rather than a distinct error; normal constraints guarantee an occurrence.
Complexity: The nested loops take O(nm) time where m is the number of occurrences, and O(n+m) space.

Task and constraints: Compute distance to the nearest occurrence of C with two directional passes.
Idea: Scan left-to-right and then right-to-left, carrying the most recent occurrence index.
Technique and why it applies: Each pass gives a one-sided nearest distance; taking the minimum of both sides yields the global nearest occurrence.
Invariant: prev is the latest occurrence in the current scan direction and result stores best distances.
Edge cases: The initial prev is set far outside the string so the first pass does not incorrectly treat index zero as a match.
Complexity: Two passes take O(n) time and O(n) result space.
